title: Vayechi: crossed hands (Genesis 48:13–20)
hook: Jacob crosses his hands to bless the younger grandson first

segments.voice: Yesterday, chesed ve'emet: true kindness, the kind that can't be repaid, like carrying Jacob home to be buried. Did you do one quiet good thing? Today, before he dies, Jacob meets two grandsons. Day two hundred eighteen.

In plenty of families, the older one gets introduced first. Gets the bigger bedroom, the first car, the photo in the middle. The younger one learns to stand a little to the side. Now here is Joseph, arranging his two sons in front of their grandfather for a blessing. He's careful. The older boy goes to Jacob's right hand, the hand of the stronger blessing. The younger goes to his left. Everything in order. And then the old man, nearly blind, does something with his arms.
screen: `THE OLDER ONE GOES FIRST.` → `JOSEPH ARRANGES HIS SONS.` → `THE OLD MAN'S ARMS.`

segments.voice: Jacob crosses his hands. His right hand goes onto the head of Ephraim, the younger. His left onto Manasseh, the firstborn. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "guiding his hands wittingly." On purpose. Joseph is upset. He takes his father's hand to move it. Not that way, father, this one's the firstborn. And Jacob says: "I know it, my son, I know it." He knows. And he doesn't stop. The younger one, he says, will be greater. But he adds something more. The older one, too, will become a people, and he too will be great. Then Jacob says: from now on, when the people of Israel bless their children, they'll say, "God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." And they do. On Friday nights, in many Jewish homes, parents place their hands on their sons' heads and say exactly that. Daughters are blessed to be like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah. Why these two boys, and not the great patriarchs? One answer some teachers give: look at the brothers before them in Genesis. Cain and Abel, Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Joseph and his brothers. Then two brothers blessed in reverse order, and the text records no quarrel between them. Another answer: they grew up in Egypt, in a palace, and stayed who they were. Genesis keeps choosing the younger. But in this scene, nobody loses. The younger one first, and the older one too.
screen: `JACOB CROSSES HIS HANDS.` · `I KNOW IT, MY SON, I KNOW IT.` · `AS EPHRAIM AND AS MANASSEH.` · `BROTHERS WHO DON'T FIGHT.` · then, large: `THE YOUNGER ONE TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the younger one. Settle, and breathe. Think of a group you're part of: a family, a team, an office, a class. Who stands a little to the side? The newest person, the quiet one, the kid who's always second. Picture them clearly. Now think of one small way to put a hand on their head, so to speak. A question just for them. Their name, said first for once. The bell holds the time.
Vayechi. The portion where the dying Jacob crosses his hands and blesses the younger grandson first, and the older one too.
Your line: the younger one too. Today, turn toward the person who usually stands to the side, and give them the first word. Day two hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: On Friday night, before the Shabbat meal, many Jewish parents bless their children with hands on their heads: sons to be like Ephraim and Manasseh, daughters like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, followed by the priestly blessing.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. your father has crossed his hands and put the stronger blessing on your younger son. what do you do?
options: take his hand to move it to the firstborn.
fork.reveal: Joseph tried to move the hand. Jacob refused: I know it, my son, I know it. and he blessed the older one to be great too.

original.note: Hebrew: God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh. The blessing for sons (Genesis 48:20).

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man got confused about which boy was which.
what it means: Jacob deliberately blesses the younger first, and still blesses the older to be great.
what a scholar hears: the Hebrew sikel et yadav, guiding his hands wittingly, comes from a root for insight; it can also be read as he crossed his hands.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 48:14, 48:19 and 48:20.

Reasons for the Ephraim and Manasseh blessing (first brothers without rivalry; kept identity in Egypt) are popular modern explanations, not attributed to a classical source; a Keeper may want to name sources or soften.
Trapdoor: sikel read as 'he crossed' (Onkelos/Rashi render it as acting wisely/deliberately; some read it as crossing); confirm framing.
Friday-night blessing custom: order (children's blessing then priestly blessing) varies by family.
